questions.q: Consider a circuit consisting of a capacitor of capacitance $C$ and a coil with $N$ turns per unit length, cross sectional area $S$ and length $d$, where $d^2 \gg S$. There is another coil of length $d/2$, cross sectional area $S/2$ and $2N$ turns per unit length completely inside the larger coil, as shown in the figure. The ends of this smaller coil are connected with each other by an insulated conducting wire. The self-inductance of the larger coil is $L$. Neglecting edge effects and all the Ohmic resistances, the resonant frequency of the circuit is:
options: $\dfrac{4}{\sqrt{15\, LC}}$
$\dfrac{6}{\sqrt{5\, LC}}$
$\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3\, LC}}$
$\sqrt{\dfrac{2}{3\, LC}}$
questions.solution:
Let the larger coil be coil 1 and the smaller coil be coil 2.

The self-inductance of the larger coil is given by:
$L_1 = \mu_0 n_1^2 A_1 l_1 = \mu_0 N^2 S d = L$

The self-inductance of the smaller coil is:
$L_2 = \mu_0 n_2^2 A_2 l_2 = \mu_0 (2N)^2 \left(\dfrac{S}{2}\right) \left(\dfrac{d}{2}\right) = \mu_0 (4N^2) \left(\dfrac{Sd}{4}\right) = \mu_0 N^2 S d = L$

The mutual inductance between the two coils is:
$M = \mu_0 n_1 n_2 A_{\text{common}} l_{\text{common}}$
Since the smaller coil is completely inside the larger coil, the common area is $S/2$ and the common length is $d/2$.
$M = \mu_0 (N) (2N) \left(\dfrac{S}{2}\right) \left(\dfrac{d}{2}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2} \mu_0 N^2 S d = \dfrac{L}{2}$

Let $i_1$ be the current in the larger coil and $i_2$ be the current in the smaller coil. The voltage across the larger coil is:
$V = L_1 \dfrac{di_1}{dt} + M \dfrac{di_2}{dt}$

Since the smaller coil is short-circuited, the net voltage across it is zero:
$0 = L_2 \dfrac{di_2}{dt} + M \dfrac{di_1}{dt} \Rightarrow \dfrac{di_2}{dt} = -\dfrac{M}{L_2} \dfrac{di_1}{dt}$

Substituting this into the first equation, we get the effective inductance $L_{\text{eq}}$:
$V = L_1 \dfrac{di_1}{dt} - \dfrac{M^2}{L_2} \dfrac{di_1}{dt} = \left( L_1 - \dfrac{M^2}{L_2} \right) \dfrac{di_1}{dt}$
$L_{\text{eq}} = L_1 - \dfrac{M^2}{L_2} = L - \dfrac{(L/2)^2}{L} = L - \dfrac{L}{4} = \dfrac{3L}{4}$

The resonant angular frequency of the circuit is:
$\omega = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{L_{\text{eq}} C}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\dfrac{3L}{4} C}} = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3LC}}$

Answer: $\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3\, LC}}$

The source voltage varies in time as $V(t)=300 \sin (400 t) \mathrm{V}$, where $t$ is time in s. List-I shows various options for the load. The possible currents $i(t)$ in the circuit as a function of time are given in List-II.

Choose the option that describes the correct match between the entries in List-I to those in List-II.
List-I List-II
$(P)$
$(1)$
$(Q)$
$(2)$
$(R)$
$(3)$
$(S)$
$(4)$

$\mathrm{P} \rightarrow 1, \mathrm{Q} \rightarrow 5, \mathrm{R} \rightarrow 2, \mathrm{~S} \rightarrow 3$
$\mathrm{P} \rightarrow 3, \mathrm{Q} \rightarrow 4, \mathrm{R} \rightarrow 2, \mathrm{~S} \rightarrow 1$
$\mathrm{P} \rightarrow 1, \mathrm{Q} \rightarrow 4, \mathrm{R} \rightarrow 2, \mathrm{~S} \rightarrow 5$

For P
$i=\frac{V}{R}=10 \sin 400 t \Rightarrow(3)$
For Q
$\begin{aligned} & X_L=\omega L=400 \times 100 \times 10^{-3}=40 \Omega \\ & \therefore Z=50 \Omega \\ & \left.\therefore i=\frac{300}{50} \sin \left(400 t-53^{\circ}\right) \text{ [current will lag by } \tan ^{-1} \frac{X_L}{R}\right] \Rightarrow(5)\end{aligned}$

Initially, both the keys are open and there is no charge on the capacitor. At an instant, key $K_1$ is closed and immediately after this the current in $R_0$ is found to be $I_1$. After a long time, the current attains a steady state value $I_2$. Thereafter, $\mathrm{K}_2$ is closed and simultaneously $\mathrm{K}_1$ is opened and the voltage across $C_0$ oscillates with amplitude $V_0$ and angular frequency $\omega_0$. Match the quantities mentioned in List-I with their values in List-II and choose the correct option.

$\mathrm{P} \rightarrow 1 ; \mathrm{Q} \rightarrow 2 ; \mathrm{R} \rightarrow 3 ; \mathrm{S} \rightarrow 5$

$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{I}_1=0 \\ & \mathrm{P} \rightarrow(1)\end{aligned}$

questions.q:
In a circuit shown in the figure, the capacitor $C$ is initially uncharged and the key $K$ is open. In this condition, a current of $1A$ flows through the $1Ω$ resistor. The key is closed at time $t = {t}_{0}$. Which of the following statement(s) is(are) correct?

[Given : ${e}^{– 1} = 0 . 36$]
options: The value of the resistance $R$ is $3Ω$
For $t < {t}_{0}$, the value of current ${I}_{1}$ is $2A$
At $t = {t}_{0} + 7 . 2\mus$, the current in the capacitor is $0 . 6A$
For $t \to \infty$, the charge on the capacitor is $12\muC$
questions.solution:
From second branch, we can see the potential drop across the branch is $5 + \left(1 \times 1\right) = 6V$.

Now for the first branch, we can write

$15 - IR = 6 . . . \left(1\right)$ and from third branch, we can write

${I}_{1} \times 3 = 6$

$⇒ {I}_{1} = 2A$

Now from Kirchoff's junction rule,

$I = {I}_{1} + 1 = 3$

Now, from equation(1), we can write

$15 - 3R = 6$

$⇒ R = 3Ω$

All three branches are in parallel, therefore we can write equivalent resistance as:

$\dfrac{1}{{R}_{eq}} = \dfrac{1}{3} + \dfrac{1}{3} + 1$

$⇒ {R}_{eq} = \dfrac{3}{5}Ω = 0 . 6Ω$

As all branches are in parallel with the capacitor branch, potential drop across all three branches will be the same. Therefore,

${E}_{eq} = 6V$.

Now, current variation in the circuit due to charging will be $\dfrac{6}{\left(\dfrac{3}{5} + 3\right)}e\dfrac{- \left(t - {t}_{0}\right)}{CR}$

At, $t = {t}_{0} + 7 . 2\mu s$, we get

$i = \dfrac{6 \times 5}{18}{e}^{- \dfrac{\left(7 . 2 \times {10}^{- 6}\right)}{\left(2 \times {10}^{- 6}\right) \times \left(3 . 6\right)}}$

$= \dfrac{30}{18} \times {e}^{- 1} = \dfrac{30}{18} \times 0 . 36$

$= 0 . 6A$

At steady state, voltage across capacitor $= 6V$.

$Q = 6 \times 2 = 12\muC$.

questions.q:
A series LCR circuit is connected to a $45sin ( \omegat )$ Volt source. The resonant angular frequency of the circuit is ${10}^{5}rad{s}^{- 1}$ and current amplitude at resonance is ${I}_{0}$. When the angular frequency of the source is $\omega = 8 \times {10}^{4}rad{s}^{- 1}$, the current amplitude in the circuit is $0 . 05{I}_{0}$. If $L = 50mH$, match each entry in List-$I$ with an appropriate value from List-$II$ and choose the correct option.

List-$I$ List-$II$
$P$ ${I}_{0}$ in $mA$ $1$ $44 . 4$
$Q$ The quality factor of the circuit $2$ $18$
$R$ The bandwidth of the circuit in $rad{s}^{- 1}$ $3$ $400$
$S$ The peak power dissipated at resonance in Watt $4$ $2250$
$5$ $500$
options: $P \to 2, Q \to 3, R \to 5, S \to 1$
$P \to 3, Q \to 1, R \to 4, S \to 2$
$P \to 4, Q \to 5, R \to 3, S \to 1$
$P \to 4, Q \to 2, R \to 1, S \to 5$
questions.solution:
Resonant angular frequency is given by, $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{LC}} = {10}^{5}$

$\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\left(50 \times {10}^{- 3}\right)C}} = {10}^{5} ⇒ C = 2 \times {10}^{- 9}F$

Given: $V = 45sin\left(\omegat\right)$. Therefore, ${V}_{0} = 45$.

Now, ${I}_{0} = \dfrac{{V}_{0}}{R} = \dfrac{45}{R} . . . \left(ii\right)$

Inductive reactance, ${X}_{L} = \omegaL = \left(8 \times {10}^{4}\right) \times \left(50 \times {10}^{- 3}\right) = 4000Ω$.

and capacitive reactance, ${X}_{C} = \dfrac{1}{\omegaC} = \dfrac{1}{\left(8 \times {10}^{4}\right) \times \left(2 \times {10}^{- 9}\right)} = 6250Ω$.

For new current amplitude, we can write

$0 . 05{I}_{0} = \dfrac{45}{\sqrt{{R}^{2} + {\left({X}_{L} - {X}_{C}\right)}^{2}}} ⇒ 0 . 05{I}_{0} = \dfrac{45}{\sqrt{{R}^{2} + {\left(6250 - 4000\right)}^{2}}} ⇒ 0 . 05 \times \dfrac{45}{R} = \dfrac{45}{\sqrt{{R}^{2} + {\left(6250 - 4000\right)}^{2}}} ⇒ {R}^{2} + {\left(6250 - 4000\right)}^{2} = \dfrac{{R}^{2}}{{\left(0 . 05\right)}^{2}} ⇒ {R}^{2} + {\left(2250\right)}^{2} = 400{R}^{2} ⇒ R = \dfrac{2250}{\sqrt{399}} = 112 . 67Ω$

Where ${X}_{{L}_{0}} = {X}_{{C}_{0}}$ are at resonant frequencies

On solving, $⇒ {I}_{0} = \dfrac{45}{R} ≃ 400mA$

Quality factor $Q = \dfrac{{X}_{L}}{R} ≃ 44 . 44$

Now, $Q = \dfrac{{\omega}_{0}}{∆ \omega} ⇒ ∆ \omega ≃ 2250rad{s}^{- 1}$.

Peak power $= 45 \times \dfrac{400}{1000}W = 18W$

Therefore, $P \to 3, Q \to 1, R \to 4, S \to 2$.

questions.q: Consider an $LC$ circuit, with inductance $L = 0 . 1H$ and capacitance $C = {10}^{- 3}F$, kept on a plane. The area of the circuit is $1{m}^{2}$. It is placed in a constant magnetic field of strength ${B}_{0}$ which is perpendicular to the plane of the circuit. At time $t = 0$, the magnetic field strength starts increasing linearly as $B = {B}_{0} + \betat$ with $\beta = 0 . 04T{s}^{- 1}$. The maximum magnitude of the current in the circuit is____$mA$.
questions.solution:
Emf induced in the circuit is

$\left|E\right| = \left|\dfrac{dϕ}{dt}\right| = \dfrac{d}{dt}\left[\left({B}_{0} + \betat\right)A\right]$

$= \beta \times A$

$= 0 . 04V$

So the circuit can be rearranged as

Using Kirchhoff's law we can write

$E = L\dfrac{di}{dt} + \dfrac{q}{C}$

$L\dfrac{di}{dt} = E - \dfrac{q}{C}$

For maximum current, $\dfrac{d i}{d t} = 0$,

Or $q = CE$

Using work energy theorem,

$qE = \dfrac{1}{2}L{i}^{2} + \dfrac{{q}^{2}}{2C}$

At ${i}_{max}$, $CEE = \dfrac{1}{2}L{i}_{max}^{2} + \dfrac{{E}^{2}{C}^{2}}{2C}$

Or, ${i}_{max} = \sqrt{\dfrac{C}{L}}E$

So, ${i}_{max} = \sqrt{\dfrac{{10}^{- 3} \times 0 . 04}{0 . 1 \times {10}^{- 3}}}$$= 4mA$

At time $t = 0$, the magnetic field strength starts increasing linearly as $B = {B}_{0} + \betat$ with $\beta = 0 . 04T{s}^{- 1}$. The maximum magnitude of the current in the circuit is____$mA$.
questions.explanation:
Emf induced in the circuit is

$\left|E\right| = \left|\dfrac{dϕ}{dt}\right| = \dfrac{d}{dt}\left[\left({B}_{0} + \betat\right)A\right]$

$= \beta \times A$

$= 0 . 04V$

So the circuit can be rearranged as

Using Kirchhoff's law we can write

$E = L\dfrac{di}{dt} + \dfrac{q}{C}$

$L\dfrac{di}{dt} = E - \dfrac{q}{C}$

For maximum current, $\dfrac{d i}{d t} = 0$,

Or $q = CE$

Using work energy theorem,

$qE = \dfrac{1}{2}L{i}^{2} + \dfrac{{q}^{2}}{2C}$

At ${i}_{max}$, $CEE = \dfrac{1}{2}L{i}_{max}^{2} + \dfrac{{E}^{2}{C}^{2}}{2C}$

Or, ${i}_{max} = \sqrt{\dfrac{C}{L}}E$

So, ${i}_{max} = \sqrt{\dfrac{{10}^{- 3} \times 0 . 04}{0 . 1 \times {10}^{- 3}}}$$= 4mA$

In a circuit, a metal filament lamp is connected in series with a capacitor of capacitance $\mathrm{C} \mu F$ across a $200 \mathrm{~V}, 50 \mathrm{~Hz}$ supply. The power consumed by the lamp is $500 \mathrm{~W}$ while the voltage drop across it is $100 \mathrm{~V}$. Assume that there is no inductive load in the circuit. Take $r m s$ values of the voltages. The magnitude of the phaseangle (in degrees) between the current and the supply voltage is $\varphi$. Assume, $\pi \sqrt{3} \approx 5$.
The value of $C$ is ____.
questions.solution:
Given,

$P = 500W$

${V}_{R} = 100V$

$f = 50Hz$

${V}_{rms} = 200V$

$P = \dfrac{{{V}_{R}}^{2}}{R} ⇒ R = \dfrac{{{V}_{R}}^{2}}{P} ⇒ R = \dfrac{{\left(100\right)}^{2}}{500}$

$∴ R = 20Ω$

Now current in the circuit,

$i = {i}_{rms} = \dfrac{voltageacrossresistor}{resistance}i = \dfrac{100}{20}i = 5A$

Phasor diagram of the given circuit for voltage,

Now,

${V}^{2} = {{V}_{C}}^{2} + {{V}_{R}}^{2} ⇒ {200}^{2} = {{V}_{C}}^{2} + {100}^{2} ⇒ {V}_{C} = 100\sqrt{3}V$

Now,

${V}_{C} = 100\sqrt{3}V = I{X}_{C} ⇒ {X}_{C} = \dfrac{100\sqrt{3}}{5} = 20\sqrt{3}Ω$

and

${X}_{C} = \dfrac{1}{\left(2\pif\right)C} ⇒ 20\sqrt{3} = \dfrac{1}{\left(2\pi \times 100\right)C} ⇒ C = 100\mu F$

From the phasor diagram,

$tan\left(ϕ\right) = \dfrac{{X}_{C}}{R} = \dfrac{20\sqrt{3}}{20} = \sqrt{3} ⇒ ϕ = 60 °$

The instantaneous voltages at three terminals marked $X, Y$ and $Z$ are given by
${V}_{X} = {V}_{0}sin ⁡ \omegat$
${V}_{Y} = {V}_{0}sin ⁡ \left(\omegat + \dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right)$ and
${V}_{Z} = {V}_{0}sin ⁡ \left(\omegat + \dfrac{4\pi}{3}\right) .$
An ideal voltmeter is configured to read rms value of the potential difference between its terminals. It is connected between points $X$ and $Y$ and then between $Y$ and $Z$ . The reading(s) of the voltmeter will be
options: Independent of the choice of the terminals
questions.solution:
Potential difference between $XandY = {V}_{X} - {V}_{Y}$

Potential difference between $YandZ = {V}_{Y} - {V}_{Z}$

Phasor of the voltages:

From phasor diagram the peak value of ${V}_{x} - {V}_{y}$ can be calculated from parallelogram law

${\left({V}_{x} - {V}_{y}\right)}_{peak} = \sqrt{{V}_{X}^{2} + {V}_{Y}^{2} + 2{V}_{X}{V}_{Y}cos\left(60\right)} = \sqrt{{V}_{0}^{2} + {V}_{0}^{2} + 2{V}_{0}{V}_{0} \times \dfrac{1}{2}} = \sqrt{3}{V}_{0}$

$∴ {\left({V}_{X} - {V}_{Y}\right)}_{peak} = \sqrt{3}{V}_{0}$

${\left({V}_{x} - {V}_{y}\right)}_{rms} = {V}_{XY}^{rms} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}{V}_{0}}{\sqrt{2}}$

Similarly  ${\left({V}_{y} - {V}_{z}\right)}_{rms} = {V}_{XY}^{rms} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}{V}_{0}}{\sqrt{2}}$

questions.q: In the circuit shown, $L = 1\text{\mu}H, C = 1\text{\mu}FandR = 1kΩ .$ They are connected in series with an a.c. source $V = {V}_{0}sin ⁡ \text{\omega}t$ as shown. Which of the following options is/are correct?
options: At  $\omega ≫ {10}^{6}rad{sec}^{- 1} ⁡$ the circuit behaves as a capacitor
The frequency at which the current will be in phase with the voltage is independent of $R$
The current will be in phase with the voltage if  $\omega = {10}^{4}rad{sec}^{- 1} ⁡$

questions.solution:
The current will be in phase with voltage when phase angle is zero,

$∴ tan ⁡ \text{ϕ} = \dfrac{\text{\omega}L - \dfrac{1}{\text{\omega}C}}{R} = 0$

Where $\text{\omega}, L, C, R$ are the angular frequency, inductance, capacitance and resistance respectively.

$⇒ \text{\omega} = {\text{\omega}}_{0} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}$

$⇒ {\text{\omega}}_{\text{ο}}$is independent of $R$

$⇒ ( resonantfrequency ) {\text{\omega}}_{0} = {10}^{6}rad / s$

Current in the circuit is given by,

${i}_{0} = \dfrac{{V}_{0}}{\sqrt{{R}^{2} + {\left(\text{\omega}L - \dfrac{1}{\text{\omega}C}\right)}^{2}}}$

When $\text{\omega} \to 0, {i}_{0} \to 0$

For $\text{\omega} ≫ {\text{\omega}}_{0}$ circuit behaves as inductor.

questions.q: Two inductors ${L}_{i}$ (inductance $1mH$, internal resistance $3Ω$ ) and ${L}_{2}$ (inductance $2mH$, internal resistance $4Ω$ ), and a resistor $R$(resistance $12Ω$ ) are all connected in parallel across a $5V$ battery. The circuit is switched on at time $t = 0$. The ratio of the maximum current $\left(\dfrac{{I}_{max}}{{I}_{min}}\right)$ drawn from the battery is:
questions.solution:
Initally, the inductances will offer infinite resistance and the current will be maximum.

${I}_{max} = \dfrac{ε}{R} = \dfrac{5}{12}A$ (Initially at t = 0)

Upon reaching steady state, the inductances will act as pure resistors and hence the current will be minimum.
${I}_{min} = \dfrac{ε}{{R}_{eq}} = ε\left(\dfrac{1}{{r}_{1}} + \dfrac{1}{{r}_{2}} + \dfrac{1}{R}\right)$ (Finally in steady state)
$= 5\left(\dfrac{1}{3} + \dfrac{1}{4} + \dfrac{1}{12}\right)$
$= \dfrac{10}{3}A$
$\dfrac{{I}_{max}}{{I}_{min}} = 8$

Voltage across the capacitors will increase from 0 to $10 \mathrm{~V}$ exponentially. The voltage at time $t$ will be given by

& \therefore \quad V=10$\left($1-e^{-t / 4}\right) \\
&

Substituting $V=4$ volt we have,

4=10$\left($1-e^{-t / 4}\right)

Substituting $V=4$ volt we have,

4=10$\left($1-e^{-t / 4}\right)

or $e^{-t / 4}=0.6=\frac{3}{5}$
Taking $\log$ both sides we have,

-$\frac{t}{4}=\ln$3-\ln 5

or $\quad t=4(\ln 5-\ln 3)=2 \mathrm{~s}$.
Hence, the answer is 2 .
